note: One term per idea, and the phrasings banned in its place (spec: kb.data.glossary). Each term holds eight fields: `id` (stable, anchors its block on the reference page), `term` (the word to write), `definition` (markdown inline text), `aliases` (also-fine words), `avoid` (banned phrasings), `scope` (a key of `scopes`: who decides the word), `owner` and `see` (related term ids, listed on both sides). Every `avoid` phrasing is banned in every markdown prose line git lists by the vocabulary gate (tools/src/gates/check-vocabulary.ts): matched whole-word and case-blind, a trailing s or es included, never inside code or on a line carrying <!-- vocab-ok -->. tools/src/gen/gen-vocabulary.ts renders docs/reference/glossary.md from this file (make glossary, or make gen). It is the single source and is edited by hand; ban a phrasing only when failing a build over it is acceptable, and never one whose words appear in a path.

scopes.kinds: The content model decides the page kinds: each fixes which blocks a page carries and the folder it lives in.
scopes.blocks: The content model decides the blocks: each answers one question, in a fixed order per kind.
scopes.verbs: The relation vocabulary decides the verbs: a closed set, each paired with its inverse and declared on both pages it joins.
scopes.polarities: The content model decides which side of a many-sided block an item argues.
scopes.properties: The data files and kb.mjs decide these: the facts recorded about a page beyond its frontmatter and the relation verbs — where kb.mjs files it (kind, band, group), the note on each edge in relations.json, and the roles and tours learning-paths.json gives it. The kb: names are this vocabulary's own; the built page's JSON-LD is a schema.org TechArticle (headline, description, keywords, isPartOf, author, dateModified) and carries none of them.
scopes.house: The house style decides these words: the owner picks the plain word, and the ban gate fails every prose line that uses a phrasing listed under Don't say.

terms.definition: A reusable solution to a recurring problem, filed at one rung of the elevation ladder or under one lens. The largest kind, and the one the other six point at.
A failure mode with a name — what goes wrong, what it costs, and which patterns keep it from happening. A hazard names the problem rather than fixing it; the fix is a `mitigated-by` hop away.
A guided tour through the patterns that answer one recurring question. A theme owns its membership: its tour steps are the source of truth, and each pattern names the theme back.
A design maxim — SOLID, DRY, KISS, YAGNI. Not a mechanism you build but a rule you honour, which is why it carries a mandatory block on how it fails when taken too far.
A worked case study — a system-design or low-level-design kata argued end to end, from requirements through the hard sub-problems. It joins the graph through `demonstrates`.
One category of managed cloud service, taking the capability as its subject and the vendors' products as evidence. It joins the graph through `implements`.
One product decision: the managed services and open-source contenders for a single capability area, side by side, compared on the conditions that decide the choice.
Frames the subject. Its heading is kind-flavoured — “The question”, “Understanding the problem” — but the anchor is `description` on every kind, so one call fetches the opener of any page.
One paragraph of expert-grade explanation in plain words, then one short example that shows the depth. On every kind; a design may leave it out.

How the happy path crosses the components, as a numbered topology walk. On an implementation pattern a sequence diagram carrying timing and the failure branches follows it; a conceptual band keeps its class-style diagram and stops there.
The named forms the pattern takes, each a card: what changes, and what that buys.
What the choice costs and what it buys, argued from both sides. On a design it reads as strengths against risks, biggest flaw named first.
When to reach for it and when not to — the reader's situation, not the pattern's features.
The smallest code that shows the mechanism working. Collapsed by default; the language selects the highlighter.
Real, well-known implementations that genuinely exemplify the pattern. Optional, and empty is a better answer than a guess.
What it takes to run: the tuning knobs, the signals to watch, what breaks first under load, and the gates before shipping.
Where the pattern shows up — the themes whose tours visit it. Hand-authored, and it must agree with the tour that owns it.
Three questions a reader can answer after the page, each with a short answer that links the element it rests on. Optional on a pattern, a hazard and a principle.
What produces the hazard — the decisions and pressures that end in this failure mode.
What the hazard costs once it lands, in the terms the person paying it feels.
How to keep it from happening, as narrative. The typed edges to the patterns that prevent it live in `relationships`.
The primary diagram and the walk through it. On a theme it maps a concrete system; on a design it is the board plus the trace from every functional requirement to the component that satisfies it.
The axes the theme's decision moves along, and what trading one for another actually costs.
The ordered walk through the theme's patterns, each step naming the role that pattern plays here. This is the source of truth for theme membership.
The decision table — the conditions that pick one member of the theme over another.
The neighbouring themes, and the line where this one stops and that one starts.
Why the principle helps — the mechanism behind the maxim, not a restatement of it.
How to honour it in practice, at the grain of a decision someone actually makes.
How it fails when taken too far. Mandatory on every principle, because a maxim with no stated limit is advice nobody can argue with.
What the system must do (functional) and how well (non-functional). Everything downstream argues from here.
Right-sizing: the interaction shape, the numbers run, and each candidate technology adopted, rejected or deferred with a reason.
The core entities and their data design — each with its role, a one-line description and a trimmed schema.
The API surface, grouped by caller, each endpoint with its method, path and contract.
One argued deep dive per non-functional requirement, each carrying its own zoom or an iterated board.
What a Mid, Senior and Staff candidate demonstrably does with this problem. A rubric, distinct from the `explain` block.
The provider-neutral taxonomy of what this category of service does. No product names — those are evidence, and they live in the mapping.
The cross-cloud table: each capability against what AWS, Azure and Google Cloud call it, or an honest “no first-party equivalent”.
The decision argued out — which option wins under which conditions, and why.
What breaks when you move between providers, and what each break costs.
The products in the running, with their licenses and whether a managed offering exists.
The contenders compared on the conditions that decide the choice, one row per condition.
The typed edges to other pages. Generated by `kb.mjs link`, declared on both pages, and the reason the graph exists.
The two are used together, each covering what the other leaves open.
Either one solves the problem, so you choose between them rather than adopting both.
The two get mistaken for each other; know the difference before you pick one.
This page is a narrower form of the target, differing in one deliberate way.
The target is a narrower form of this page, differing in one deliberate way.
This page narrows the target to one case — a tighter pattern, or a product comparison sitting under the capability area it compares within.
This page is the wider subject that the target narrows to one case.
You cannot adopt this page without the target already in place, which is why it renders as Requires.
Having this page in place is what makes the target possible.
The target is one of the parts this page is built from.
This page is one of the parts the target is built from.
Adopting this page keeps the target hazard from happening, which is why it renders as Prevents.
The target is what you adopt to keep this hazard from happening.
This pattern or design is open to the target hazard: the hazard acts on its own mechanism, so the page needs a guard against it.
This hazard acts on the target pattern or design, so that page needs a guard against it.
This worked case study puts the target to use, so you can read the pattern at work in a real system.
The target is a worked case study that puts this page to use.
This service category or product comparison ships the target ready-made, so you can buy or run it instead of building it.
The target is a service category or set of products you can get this page ready-made from.
An argument for adopting the page's subject — what it buys you.
An argument against — what it costs, stated as a fact rather than hedged.
A situation that calls for the pattern, written as the reader's circumstance.
A situation where reaching for it makes things worse.
A configuration surface you actually turn — a named parameter, or a dial described without attributing it to a product.
An observable quantity worth watching: queue depth, replication lag, p99 latency.
What breaks first under load, and how it looks when it does.
A gate to clear before shipping.

Which of the seven page kinds this is — `pattern`, `hazard`, `theme`, `principle`, `design` (a worked case study), `capability` (a category of managed cloud service), or `comparison` (a product decision: managed services and open-source contenders side by side).
The band the page declares. On a pattern that is one of the thirteen elevation bands or lenses, and also its folder; on every other kind it repeats `kb:kind`, because those pages are filed by kind.
The subdivision within a band, on the two bands that have one; elsewhere it repeats `kb:band`. It names the folder except where a group carries an alias and shares another's.
Why two things relate, from this side. Each side may phrase it its own way; only the edge and its verb must agree.
What a pattern does in the service of one particular theme.
A theme whose tour visits this pattern. The inverse of `kb:tours`.
A pattern this theme's tour visits. The inverse of `kb:in-theme`.

Where a page sits on the way in: intro, core or advanced. Recorded in docs/data/tracks.json for every theme a Start-here track stages, never in the page's frontmatter; it orders a track and says nothing about the page's depth of reading.
The plain verb for putting something to work; for the noun, name the payoff itself.
Says what something is for; the longer form adds two words and nothing else.
Says a thing is able to do something, in one word.
Says there are several without counting them; when you know the count, write the number instead.
Says what happens next, in the plain word.
Says one thing makes another easier; say let when it makes it possible.
Says a system hands out a new id, key, token or number; say generate when it computes one from scratch.
Says a value is worked out from others; choose the word for the sense — work out, build from, or rebuild by replay.
Says a value was worked out from others rather than stored or typed in; choose the word for the sense.
Says a value follows from others, so nobody needs to store or type it.
A class that extends another and inherits its members.

The project's name, in full at its first mention and "the Atlas" after it; "the KB" stays the plain noun for the knowledge base. An old name appears only inside a code span that records the history ([branding.md](../../.claude/rules/branding.md)).
